'''Peter S. Kim''' (born April 27, 1958) is an American scientist. He was president of [[Merck Research Laboratories]] (MRL) 2003–2013 and is currently Virginia & D.K. Ludwig [[Professor]] of [[Biochemistry]] at [[Stanford University]], Institute Scholar at Stanford ChEM-H, and Investigator at the [[Chan Zuckerberg Biohub]].<ref>{{cite news|title=MERCK RESEARCH LABS CHIEF PETER KIM TO JOIN STANFORD'S DEPARTMENT OF BIOCHEMISTRY|url=https://engineering.stanford.edu/research-profile/merck-research-labs-chief-peter-kim-join-stanford%E2%80%99s-department-biochemistry|access-date=27 January 2014|newspaper=Stanford Engineering|date=13 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemh.stanford.edu/people/institute-scholars|title=Institute Scholars {{!}} ChEM-H|website=chemh.stanford.edu|access-date=2019-02-05}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.czbiohub.org/people3/cz-biohub-scientific-leadership/|title=CZ Biohub Scientific Leadership – Chan Zuckerberg Biohub|language=en-US|access-date=2019-02-05|archive-date=February 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015556/https://www.czbiohub.org/people3/cz-biohub-scientific-leadership/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.stanford.edu/2016/10/26/biochemist-peter-kim-leads-chan-zuckerberg-biohub-project/|title=Biochemist Peter Kim leads Chan Zuckerberg Biohub project|last=University|first=Stanford|date=2016-10-26|website=Stanford News|language=en|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> Earlier, he was Professor of Biology at MIT, a Member of the Whitehead Institute, and an HHMI Investigator.

Kim is an elected member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], [[National Academy of Medicine]], and [[National Academy of Engineering]] known for leadership in the discovery and development of novel drugs and vaccines used worldwide.

==Early life and education==
Kim is of [[Korean American|Korean]] descent. Kim grew up in [[Ridgewood, New Jersey|Ridgewood]], [[New Jersey]], the son of a [[single mother]]. His first job was in 1974 at a [[Roy Rogers Restaurants|Roy Rogers]] restaurant, where he earned money to pay for college.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/03/11/business/my-first-job-howdy-buckaroo-heres-your-apron.html|title=MY FIRST JOB; Howdy, Buckaroo, Here's Your Apron|last=Kim|first=Dr Peter S.|date=2001-03-11|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-02-20|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Kim earned his [[A.B.]] in chemistry at [[Cornell University]] in 1979 where he conducted research with the late George P. Hess.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2012/04/biophysicist-george-hess-be-honored-april-18|title=Seminar to honor biophysicist George Hess April 18|website=Cornell Chronicle|language=en|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> He received his [[Ph.D.]] in biochemistry at [[Stanford University]] under the guidance of Robert L. ("Buzz") Baldwin.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=63909|title=Chemistry Tree – Robert Lesh Baldwin|website=academictree.org|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref>

==Career and research==
After his PhD, Kim was appointed by [[David Baltimore]] as one of the early Whitehead Fellows at the [[Whitehead Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wi.mit.edu/people/fellows|title=Whitehead Institute – Fellows Program|website=wi.mit.edu|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> Later, Kim was a professor of biology at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), a Member of the [[Whitehead Institute]] and an investigator at the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://profiles.stanford.edu/peterkim|title=Peter S. Kim's Profile {{!}} Stanford Profiles|website=profiles.stanford.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref>

Kim is known for his studies of coiled coils and for discovering how [[protein]]s cause viral membranes to fuse with [[Cell (biology)|cells]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://discovermagazine.com/1995/jun/kimscoils520|title=Kim's Coils {{!}} DiscoverMagazine.com|website=Discover Magazine|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/05/21/us/a-key-to-flu-virus-infection-is-identified.html|title=A Key to Flu Virus Infection Is Identified|last=Leary|first=Warren E.|date=1993-05-21|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-02-20|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1993/05/21/influenzas-burglary-tools/013f859b-495f-4ccd-88dd-6b1dc96df0c8/|title=INFLUENZA'S BURGLARY TOOLS|last=Rensberger|first=Boyce|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=May 21, 1993}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/library/national/science/aids/041997sci-aids.html|title=Scientists Find a Key Weapon Used by H.I.V.|website=archive.nytimes.com|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hhmi.org/news/key-hiv-protein-structure-solved|title=Key HIV Protein Structure Solved|website=HHMI.org|language=en|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> The "spring-loaded mechanism" for viral membrane fusion laid the foundation for protein-engineering efforts aimed at stabilizing the metastable native state of membrane-fusion proteins, a critical feature of several vaccines, including those for SARS-CoV-2. He has a special interest in [[HIV/AIDS]] research and designed compounds that stop membrane fusion by HIV, thereby preventing it from infecting cells, and has pioneered efforts to develop an HIV [[vaccine]] based on similar principles. Kim also served as a member of the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH) AIDS Vaccine Research Committee.<ref name="auto"/>

Kim joined Merck Research Laboratories (MRL) in 2001 as executive vice president, Research and Development.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB976056590532136963|title=Merck Names Biologist From MIT As Head of Research Operations|last=Journal|first=Gardiner HarrisStaff Reporter of The Wall Street|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=December 6, 2000 |language=en-US|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> He was promoted to president in January 2003.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2002-12-15/mercks-new-alchemist|title=Merck's New Alchemist|newspaper=Bloomberg|date=December 16, 2002 |access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> In this role Kim oversaw all of Merck's drug and vaccine research and development activities.

During his tenure, Merck gained approval of more than 20 new medicines and vaccines. These include [[Januvia]] (the first DPP-4 inhibitor for [[type 2 diabetes]]), [[Gardasil]] (the first vaccine for prevention of [[cervical cancer]]), [[Isentress]] (the first HIV integrase inhibitor), [[Zostavax]] (the first vaccine for the prevention of [[shingles]] in adults), and [[Rotateq]] (an oral vaccine for the prevention of [[rotavirus]] infection in infants). He also led the biomarker-based development of [[Pembrolizumab|Keytruda]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/davidshaywitz/2017/07/26/the-startling-history-behind-mercks-new-cancer-blockbuster/|title=The Startling History Behind Merck's New Cancer Blockbuster|last=Shaywitz|first=David|website=Forbes|language=en|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> In 2013, he retired from Merck and was succeeded by [[Roger Perlmutter]].<ref name="Perlmutter announcement">{{cite news|last=Thomas|first=Katie|title=Merck Replaces Its Research Chief|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/03/08/business/merck-replaces-its-research-chief.html?_r=0|access-date=30 November 2013|newspaper=The New York Times|date=7 March 2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bizjournals.com/philadelphia/blog/john-george/2013/03/key-merck-official-retiring-big-shoes.html|title=Key Merck official retiring, big shoes to fill|website=www.bizjournals.com|access-date=2019-02-20}}</ref> He was appointed to the faculty at [[Stanford University]] in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Goldman |first1=Bruce |date=2016-06-09 |title=Merck Research Labs chief Peter Kim to join Biochemistry |url=https://engineering.stanford.edu/news/merck-research-labs-chief-peter-kim-join-stanford-s-department-biochemistry |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009075305/https://engineering.stanford.edu/news/merck-research-labs-chief-peter-kim-join-stanford-s-department-biochemistry |archive-date=2018-10-09 |access-date=2019-02-20 |website=Stanford School of Engineering |language=en}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Kim is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[National Academy of Medicine]], the [[National Academy of Engineering]], and a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]. Other honors include:

*[[NAS Award in Molecular Biology]] (1993)
*[[Eli Lilly Award in Biological Chemistry]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.divbiolchem.org/awards/recipients/|title=Recipients &#124; ACS Division of Biological Chemistry Website|website=www.divbiolchem.org|access-date=May 14, 2020|archive-date=April 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190423183258/http://www.divbiolchem.org/awards/recipients/|url-status=dead}}</ref> (1994)
*DuPont Merck Young Investigator Award of the [[Protein Society]] (1994)
*[[Ho-Am Prize in Science|Samsung Foundation Ho-Am Prize in Basic Science]] (1998)
*The Hans Neurath Award of the [[Protein Society]] (1999)
*Doctor of Science, Honoris Causa, [[Pohang University of Science and Technology]] (2011)
*The Arthur Kornberg and Paul Berg Lifetime Achievement Award in Biomedical Sciences, [[Stanford University]] (2018)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://chemh.stanford.edu/stanford-medicine-alumni-awards-2018-peter-kim|title=Stanford Medicine Alumni Awards 2018: Peter Kim {{!}} ChEM-H|website=chemh.stanford.edu|access-date=2019-02-05|archive-date=September 11, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190911102520/https://chemh.stanford.edu/stanford-medicine-alumni-awards-2018-peter-kim|url-status=dead}}</ref>
